strategies.name: Rice – Rice (current)
strategies.summary: Rice in both Maha and Yala seasons, which needs plenty of water in both seasons.

reasons: Rice in Yala (Apr–Aug) usually needs irrigation here: average rain is about 51 mm/month (NASA POWER, adjusted -20%), below the 150 mm rule-of-thumb for a high-water crop.
Rice in Maha (Oct–Feb) usually needs irrigation here: average rain is about 144 mm/month (NASA POWER, adjusted -20%), below the 150 mm rule-of-thumb for a high-water crop.
In this illustrative case, Yala rice would likely lack water.
This is the pattern many farms already follow when tank water is available for Yala.

indicators.label: Water needed
indicators.explanation: Rice usually needs standing water, and the Yala crop grows through the driest months.

indicators.label: Soil cover through the year
indicators.explanation: Two crops keep the field covered for most of the year.

indicators.label: Natural nitrogen added
indicators.explanation: Rice does not add nitrogen; it depends on fertiliser and soil reserves.

indicators.label: Exposure to dry spells
indicators.explanation: A Yala rice crop can fail if tank water runs short.

indicators.label: Range of products to sell
indicators.explanation: One crop type means one market. No price data was used.

notes: NASA POWER shows June–August is the driest part of the year here, so Yala rice relies on stored water.
Field is bare for short periods between seasons.

benefits.text: Familiar crop with known methods, equipment and markets.
Rice tolerates waterlogged paddy soils well.

risks.text: High chance of Yala rice failure under hotter, drier conditions.
Yala rice may be lost or reduced in years when tanks do not fill.
Growing the same crop repeatedly can build up pests, diseases and weeds.

explanation.summary: This is your current pattern. It is shown so you can compare the alternatives against what you already do.
details: Rainfall data shows most rain falls October–December, which supports Maha rice.
Yala rice grows mostly in months with little rain, so stored water matters most.

strategies.name: Rice – Mung bean
strategies.summary: Keep rice in Maha, then grow quick mung bean in early Yala using less water.

steps.notes: Rest period before Maha land preparation.

reasons: Rice in Maha (Oct–Feb) usually needs irrigation here: average rain is about 144 mm/month (NASA POWER, adjusted -20%), below the 150 mm rule-of-thumb for a high-water crop.
Mung bean may still be possible if planted right after harvest to use early rains.
Mung bean is a short crop that can use April–May rains after the Maha harvest.

indicators.label: Water needed
indicators.explanation: Mung bean generally needs much less water than a second rice crop.

indicators.label: Soil cover through the year
indicators.explanation: The field is bare from July to September.

indicators.label: Natural nitrogen added
indicators.explanation: Legumes can work with soil bacteria to add some nitrogen.

indicators.label: Exposure to dry spells
indicators.explanation: A short crop finishes before the driest months.

indicators.label: Range of products to sell
indicators.explanation: Adds a second product. No price data was used.

notes: April–May average roughly 100–120 mm of rain per month (NASA POWER), which a short legume may use, but dry spells still happen.
Bare from July to September unless a cover crop is added.

benefits.text: Uses less water than Yala rice, which matters in years when tanks are low.
As a legume, mung bean may add nitrogen for the next rice crop.
Changing crops can interrupt rice pest and weed cycles.

risks.text: Heat and dry spells could reduce mung bean yields.
Mung bean is damaged by waterlogging; paddy fields need good drainage.
Heavy rain at harvest can spoil pods.
Market price and seed availability were not checked.

explanation.summary: This option lowers water needs in Yala by swapping the second rice crop for a fast legume.
details: NASA POWER rainfall shows a smaller rainy period in April–May before the dry months.
A crop of about 60–90 days could fit in that window, depending on the variety.
explanation.technical: Illustrative demo strategy. Indicator ratings are hand-prepared, not model outputs.

Local buyers and prices for mung bean.
Availability of a suitable short-duration variety.

localChecks: Ask the agricultural extension officer which mung bean varieties are recommended locally.
Check whether your field can be drained after Maha harvest.
Ask local buyers about demand before planting.

strategies.name: Rice – Cowpea – Sunn hemp cover
strategies.summary: Rice in Maha, hardy cowpea in Yala, then a sunn hemp cover crop to protect and feed the soil.

steps.notes: Turned into the soil before Maha land preparation.

reasons: You told us Sunn hemp (cover crop) seed is not available.
Rice in Maha (Nov–Mar) usually needs irrigation here: average rain is about 120 mm/month (NASA POWER, adjusted -20%), below the 150 mm rule-of-thumb for a high-water crop.
Cowpea is hardy, but the cover crop is unlikely without water.
The sunn hemp cover crop grows in the driest months and may establish poorly without some water.

indicators.label: Water needed
indicators.explanation: Cowpea and sunn hemp generally cope with dry conditions.

indicators.label: Soil cover through the year
indicators.explanation: The field stays covered nearly all year.

indicators.label: Exposure to dry spells
indicators.explanation: Cowpea is hardy, but the cover crop depends on scarce rain.

indicators.label: Range of products to sell
indicators.explanation: Cowpea adds a product; sunn hemp is for the soil, not for sale.

notes: July–September rainfall is low (NASA POWER), so the cover crop may need supplementary water to establish.
Continuous cover can reduce erosion and weed growth.

benefits.text: Keeps the soil covered all year, which can reduce erosion and weeds.
Cowpea tolerates heat and dry spells better than many crops.
Turning in sunn hemp adds organic matter to the soil.

risks.text: The cover crop would probably need to be dropped.
The cover crop may fail in a very dry July–September.
Extra work and seed cost for a crop that is not sold.
Cowpea, like mung bean, does not tolerate waterlogging.

explanation.summary: This option focuses on soil health by adding two legumes and keeping the ground covered.
details: Rainfall data shows a dry gap from June to September; the cover crop is placed in that gap, which is why it needs review.
Benefits to soil build up over several seasons, not immediately.
explanation.technical: Illustrative demo strategy with feasibility flagged for review because cover-crop months coincide with the lowest observed rainfall.
